paragraphs.text: I had never called my sister at midnight.
But the minute John Mulaney, the impish host of last week’s “Saturday Night Live,” uttered the word “sister,” I picked up the phone.
“Are you watching this?” I asked Peggy.
“Yeah, it’s not funny,” she replied. “It’s hitting too close to home.”

We hung up to experience a flashback to a decade engulfed by caring for our mother. In the sketch, Mulaney plays a man mulling how to care for his aging dad without a nursing home or a costly private health aide.

“That’s when I heard about ‘Sister,’” Mulaney says brightly. “‘Sister’ is a live-in 24-7 elder care provider that is completely free, and also your sister. Now I don’t have to worry about Dad getting the care and attention he needs, because my sister will do it, and I can get back to my life and the stuff I like to do.”
“I love my mom more than anything,” another man says. “That doesn’t mean I want to help her in the bathroom. Sister doesn’t, either, but she will, whereas I won’t.”
A third man says “Sister” won’t affect your inheritance: “You’ll still get 50 percent of the house she’s currently deep cleaning.”

It’s also a good bonding opportunity for father and son, Mulaney’s character says. He agrees with Dad that Sister’s a “bitch” after she tries to curb Dad’s salt intake to help with his high blood pressure.

When I tried to curb my mom’s salt intake, she gave me a withering look and said, “I’m 97,” before shaking the saltshaker so hard the top flew off. She kept eating because she liked a little food with her salt.

The “S.N.L.” sketch sparked a million palavers about the fact that America’s strategy for elder care often defaults to the kindness of daughters. As we’ve been startled to learn lately, a lot of our infrastructure systems are shaky and stitched together haphazardly. (Fixing one router in Arkansas should not shut down America’s whole airspace.)

The viral hit surprised me because I thought things would have changed by now, 20 years after my mom died, with a couple of generations of men raised by working women less prone to live by outdated gender roles. But, as I always say, men are evolving a lot slower than women.

“We give little girls baby dolls to play with, to train them to be caregivers, where we don’t do that for little boys,” said Jessica Calarco, a sociology professor at the University of Wisconsin and the author of “Holding It Together: How Women Became America’s Safety Net.”

“Women are making less than men in most fields and so it becomes sort of easy to assume that it’s not only natural but also logical for women to be the ones doing this kind of work when care becomes this hot potato.”
I was a bad nurse. I focused on making Mom look stylish and pretty, with eyebrow tints and pedicures and silk and velvet jackets, working on the premise that if you look good, you feel good.

“You treat her like she’s a doll,” my brother Kevin said with an accusatory look. But my mom was beautiful, with porcelain skin and snowy hair, and she loved looking good. She was blind the last seven years of her life, so she asked me to put on her red lipstick.

“You’re not doing it right,” she complained. “You’re not doing it like Max Factor.” It turned out that she had actually once had her lipstick applied by Max Factor, himself, when he was just starting out and exhibiting his new makeup line in a Washington drugstore.
Just as my three brothers had fewer household tasks growing up, they knew my sister and I would take care of Mom.

My brothers were great, but they focused on the less onerous, less “maternal” jobs. Michael brought dinner every week. Martin often came over to take Mom out to lunch, gossip about the family or read fun newspaper clippings to her. Kevin watched “Seinfeld” with her.

Peggy and I didn’t resent their doing less. Mom adored her sons, and they adored her back. But it’s often harder for men to see their parents get frail — and people are living a lot longer now. My mother’s growing helplessness — blind and in a wheelchair — made my brothers feel helpless.

“It’s also expediency with a lot of guys,” Kevin told me. “They have a life and they can’t interrupt a good part of it to alter their schedules. But I was always inclined to tell myself, ‘This happened on your watch and it’s your problem.’”

While more of my mom’s friends who had only sons ended up in nursing homes, some men are amazing caretakers. Kevin and his sons, especially his youngest, Brian, have spent years tenderly caring for Kevin’s lovely wife, Ellen, who has M.S.

When my mom’s health problems grew more severe — she once broke her neck trying to go to the bathroom in the middle of the night — we got round-the-clock help. We lied and told her it was paid for by Medicare so she wouldn’t feel sad about draining her bank account. She was living, after all, on a police widow’s pension.

Peggy and I continued to spend an enormous amount of time with her. We both had demanding jobs that required a lot of travel, and I remember feeling guilty that I couldn’t travel as much as I needed to.

It was stressful and I sometimes gave up on my own grooming; I spent way too much time in black yoga pants. But the way you exit relationships shows character. And my mom was not a whiner. She managed her pain — and sadness about losing her sight — with two bourbon and sodas in the late afternoon. (When I gave her a bottle of Maker’s Mark, she hid it in her underwear drawer; it was too fancy to drink.)
If you read her a book or a newspaper or even just ads about sales on food and fashion, she was content.
One day, I told her there was a sale at Saks on control top panties.
She looked intrigued. “Who do they control?” she asked.

She was so warm and funny, it felt like a gift to spend her last years with her. I was glad I was on hand when she fell or fainted. The Bethesda-Chevy Chase Rescue Squad was there in a flash; she never missed its annual oyster roast. I still shudder, though, when I hear a siren from an ambulance speeding through her old neighborhood.
I was happy to be there when her fading memory scared her.

One night, watching “Gone With the Wind,” she began crying because she couldn’t remember the plot of her favorite movie. I hugged her, knowing that I wouldn’t remember the plot, either, on the off chance I made it to 97.
I was happy to be on hand to straighten her out if she got confused and thought she wasn’t in her own home, or thought, because my dad wasn’t there, that he had left her for another woman.
“No,” I reassured her, “he’s waiting for you in heaven.”
There was one particular moment that made it all worth it. Late at night, when she couldn’t sleep, I held her hand.
“I love you,” she softly said. “Very much.”
At the end, as she had her last dose of morphine, with a bourbon chaser, her three sons huddled around her bed, crying. Then they left and my sister and I curled up with her.

Even though it was July, I played Christmas music because she loved it. When “Sisters,” the Rosemary Clooney-Vera-Ellen classic from “White Christmas,” came on, Peggy and I sang along. “Caring, sharing. … All kinds of weather, we stick together.” We knew all the words by heart.
